items.title: What I Learned at a Drunk-Math Party
items.description: A t 7 o’clock on a Saturday in October, the light is dimming in Cole Valley and a group of the AI industry’s young stars is gathered on the second story of a century-old Edwardian. At first glance, it looks like any other San Francisco house party: bottles of cheap liquor on the table and awkward conversations in the living room. But there are signs that this party is different. In the kitchen sits a pile of sharp No. 2 pencils and stacks of white paper. I am drinking vodka and reviewing trigonometry. The unit circle is confusing enough as it is, but it’s even worse when you are three shots in. I am here for a “drunk deriving” party. The plan is to compete against one another in math. We are going to see who, while drunk, can score highest on a set of past problems from Oxford’s math-and-computer-science undergraduate-entrance exam. Normally this exam is taken individually, but for the party, the host sorts us into teams based on our self-professed math abilities. Asking AI researchers and start-up founders who spend their evenings at math parties to rate themselves on quantitative skill is a dicey proposition: Even those who majored in the field will report that they are bad for fear that an International Mathematical Olympiad medalist is in the room. But as a writer among mostly programmers, I figure that no one is expecting much from me. I am placed on a team with a guy who studied theoretical physics as a Rhodes Scholar. Once everyone is drunk, the host sends out the exam, a 13-page document with both multiple-choice and long-answer questions. Not only are we competing against one another; a parallel party is taking place in New York City. The winning team will be the one with the highest combined blood-alcohol levels and exam score. We have two and a half hours to complete the test, and calculators are banned. My two teammates start by tackling the multiple-choice items, a grab bag of logarithms and polynomials. I start with Question 6, a logic problem that mercifully has no numbers. It’s a Holmesian mystery about a shattered vase and four deceitful friends: Alice blames Bob, who blames Diane, who says Bob is wrong, and Charlie claims it wasn’t him. “Explain why at least one of the four must be lying,” instructs the exam. How strange , I think, to be doing math recreationally in the place where it’s all being automated . San Francisco is a city steeped in mathematics. The landscape, with its roller-coaster hills and valleys, is sinusoidal. People speak quantitatively too. At coffee shops in Pacific Heights, investors talk about scaling laws and S-curves and hockey-stick charts with exponential growth. Everything is riding on the tech industry’s improbable main bet: If machines can be taught to improve themselves ad infinitum, that will set off an age of impossible growth. The median Anthropic employee’s beliefs suggest an economy expanding by 17 percent annually by the end of the decade. Private-company valuations run into the trillions. In math, numbers can be natural, irrational, p-adic, and surreal. Here they simply feel made-up. Lately, the city’s math fixation has become literal. “What is it that mathematicians even do?” a young man across from me on the bus recently asked his friend as we heaved up Fillmore. His seatmate nodded philosophically. They were discussing AI models’ rapid progress in mathematics. At first the problems fell slowly: the unit-distance problem, the Jacobian conjecture, Navier-Stokes. Then came The Dump. In early October, OpenAI announced an internal model had obtained hundreds of mathematical results across more than a dozen subfields. A deluge of new AI-generated solutions has continued unabated ever since. Like the men on the bus, I too have recently become a bandwagon math fan. My fascination started over the summer after Jacob Tsimerman, one of this year’s Fields Medalists, warned me about the scale of the impending transformation. The day before the drunk-math party, I took the Caltrain south from San Francisco to Stanford to hang out with a pair of fifth-year math Ph.D.s who are thinking specifically about how AI is reshaping their discipline. I met with Henry Bosch, a geometer, and Shurui Liu, who works on a mysterious, constellational project called the Langlands program. The coffee shop where I met them is wedged inside Stanford’s electrical-engineering building, several hundred feet from the auditorium where, as a freshman, I took my last math exam. This put an end to a troubling 10-week course in multivariable calculus and linear algebra—the math underlying large language models—and also to my formal math studies. People study math for all kinds of reasons. Some have an aptitude for it and get high on the problem-solving. Bosch, an enthusiastic, restless man in clear-framed glasses and jeans, decided to pursue the subject in high school after his statistician father gave him a copy of Baby Rudin, an undergraduate textbook written by a Jewish Viennese exile—Walter Rudin. (Don’t be fooled by the nickname: The textbook, which is actually titled Principles of Mathematical Analysis , is famously terse.) Liu, who showed up dressed in a black Temu T-shirt printed with an esoteric computer-science joke, is as romantic as they come. When he was in elementary school, he was bad at math. He fell in love with it only after a depressive phase as a 14-year-old in northeastern China. “I could not sleep for several days. I was really worried that after I die, everything will become emptiness,” Liu recounted. His angst led him to theoretical physics, and that eventually brought him to math. Like many mathematicians, Liu delights in the subject’s purity: “Math allows you to build your own mental model of the universe,” he told me. In talking about their sadness at watching AI solve long-standing proofs, many mathematicians describe the subject as akin to art . Yet most of us grow up to develop the opposite associations. Mathematical beauty—“a beauty cold and austere, like that of sculpture,” as the philosopher Bertrand Russell described it—is assumed inaccessible. So while paintings and marbles are studied in crowded museum galleries, mathematical beauty is appreciated primarily by research mathematicians in their private sanctuaries. The typical math curriculum trains students to be problem solvers but fails to instill the romance that compels Liu. Now, as the machines keep improving, some mathematicians say beauty is being lost while others say a new kind of beauty is being born. They have started speaking about the crisis the way soldiers must have spoken of the French Revolution: It’s all been terribly violent or fantastically radical. “It was but a pellet of lead in a shotgun blast,” one lamented in response to an AI proof for a problem he has worked on for two decades. But Liu has kept his romantic streak. “I think AI will accelerate our understanding of the universe,” he said. When it’s supposed to rain in California, that’s all anyone talks about. The day I met Edward Frenkel was one of those days. (“Are you excited for the rain?” my curly-haired Irish neighbor asked me as I passed by him on the sidewalk.) Frenkel lives in the sloping Berkeley Hills, not far from the group houses filled with people who sincerely believe the world is about to end. This unusually depressive California weather would be apt for the apocalypse , I thought on the drive over. When I arrived, Frenkel opened the door in flip-flops and a T-shirt from a club in Ibiza. There was a DJ setup and a disco ball in his book-lined living room. The room’s windows revealed a panoramic view of the blue bay, and beyond, the endless Pacific. Had I not known Frenkel to be a world-class mathematician, I would have thought him to be a surfer. Frenkel reminded me of an older, more settled Liu. Growing up during the Cold War in the U.S.S.R., he was enchanted by quantum physics, which eventually led him to math, a subject he hadn’t cared for as a child. When he applied for entrance to Moscow’s top math program at age 16, he was denied on account of his father being Jewish. But he persisted, climbing over the university’s fence to sneak into lectures. By 21, he was a visiting professor at Harvard. Years later, he moved to Berkeley, where he has taught for three decades. Frenkel studies the Langlands program, same as Liu, a decades-long effort to connect far-flung and seemingly disparate subfields: a sort of grand unified theory of math. Alongside his research, he has made a career as a math evangelist. He wrote his 2013 book, Love and Math , to make the field’s beauty accessible to the public (“eros pervades his winsome new memoir,” one reviewer wrote at the time). Frenkel once caused a stir on campus by writing and starring in an erotic math film. One of Frenkel’s obsessions is the question of where math comes from. The objects that make up the mathematical world have bizarre properties. Consider an infinite line—we have never encountered one (the observable universe is finite) and yet we can reason together about them. The same applies to more complicated mathematical objects such as sheaves or Galois groups. Stranger yet, these mathematical objects sometimes end up describing the real world in unforeseen ways: An abstract concept first established in mathematics might become central to explaining physical phenomena decades or even centuries later. Complex numbers (which have both real and imaginary parts) were first conceived of in the 16th century but proved foundational to the development of quantum mechanics in the 1920s. So where do these mathematical objects reside? Is math something we are inventing collectively, like the Greek language, or does it exist independently of us and we are discovering it, as the Polynesians once encountered the Hawaiian Islands? (“Look, there on the horizon—a new number system!”) There is no settled answer. But Frenkel posits that mathematics is a bridge that connects our minds to reality. He has put forth a labyrinthine theory that mathematical concepts reside in the same collective unconscious proposed by the psychologist Carl Jung in the early 20th century. “I am convinced that there are deeper structures which we have not even seen yet; we cannot even imagine what they are,” Frenkel told me. This theory is desperately speculative. (“That’s a hypothesis,” he emphasized as he slurped the duck noodle soup we ordered from a nearby Thai place.) But the core idea is that mathematics is intrinsically linked to human interiority. In recent months, mathematics has proved particularly vulnerable to automation. This is partly because the field is now so expansive. Top mathematicians once made contributions across many subfields, but over the past century, the discipline has swelled such that no one has a full grasp of it. In some of AI’s most impressive work so far, the models have solved problems by connecting existing concepts: “The proof is a surprising synthesis of well-known ideas,” one mathematician explained to Quanta in describing OpenAI’s machine-generated proof of the quasi-Riemann hypothesis. But AI’s progress in math also owes itself to the fact that math is ruthlessly objective. If a computer were to produce Swann’s Way , we could deny its genius on the grounds that it was generated by a machine. In mathematics, there’s no such room for dispute. But perhaps math does have more in common with art than is typically accepted. Matilde Marcolli, a mathematical physicist at Caltech, sees it both as a way of making sense of reality and as a form of self-expression: “Your mathematics, that is like the poem that composes itself in the mind and explodes onto the page because your life demands it,” she writes. Frenkel likes to cite William James’s declaration that science’s denial of its practitioners’ individuality would eventually look shortsighted. Perhaps it is wishful thinking to believe that the human mind remains in some ways exceptional— Never say never , the mathematicians all now solemnly hedge—but it is certainly the case that humans can do all sorts of things that machines cannot. “When we fall in love, we actually experience infinity in some sense,” Frenkel told me. Computers cannot experience heartbreak or dance the waltz. Nor, for that matter, can computers take drunk-math exams and laugh with their friends inside sweaty San Francisco apartments. “We are infinite in our capacities,” Frenkel said. When I finish the logic question, I feel delighted with my solution, not in the way of cosmic beauty, which motivates Frenkel and Liu, but a more elementary satisfaction at having completed the problem—even if a machine would have done it faster. And although I don’t much like alcohol or math, the truth is that I am having a lot of fun. Drunk deriving (this refers to the logical process used to arrive at certain mathematical results) is certainly less common than drunk driving (which, here in San Francisco, now means pregaming Modelos in a Waymo). There is strong precedent for doing math under the influence though. At a chandeliered cafe in 1930s Lviv, mathematicians including Stefan Banach, Stanisław Ulam, and John von Neumann advanced the field over coffee and cognac. “The food was average, but there were plenty of drinks,” writes Ulam, who describes wide-ranging conversations on math alongside discussions of politics and astronomy. But standardized-math-exam parties are an idea that could have been born only in the tortured minds of 21st-century overachievers. With my teammates lost in a tangle of derivatives, I move on to a problem about calendar dates. The task is to find the most recent date before today without repeated digits. (For instance, 12/07/1974 has two sets of repeated digits—1 and 7—but 03/25/1974 has none.) I am quite drunk and my math faculties are in decline, but the answer, I determine, through a stubborn and inelegant process, must be 06/25/1987. June 25, 1987, was a hot day in Washington, and at a ceremony in the Rose Garden, President Ronald Reagan awarded medals to a selection of the country’s top scientists and technologists. Among the recipients were Robert Noyce, a co-founder of Intel, for his work inventing computer chips, and Michael Freedman, a mathematician at UC San Diego, for advances in topology that won him the Fields Medal. At the ceremony, Reagan quoted Benjamin Franklin, who once, marveling at the speed of 18th-century advance, wrote that he almost wished he had instead been born two or three centuries later. Noyce passed away a few years afterward—he would never fully see the world that Intel built—but Freedman is now in his 70s and works as the chief science officer at an AI start-up called Logical Intelligence. This spring, Freedman published a paper on AI and mathematics that argues that machines might help us make progress on the age-old problem of whether math is discovered or invented—the same question that interests Frenkel. “Humans will not stop doing mathematics,” he and his co-authors write. They expect the field to grow more popular instead. The calendar problem asks me when the next date without repeating digits will occur. The answer I find is June 17, 2345—which seems impossibly far off. Like Franklin awed by the rapid progress of his time, I wish I could see the world three centuries in the future. Then again, the present already feels surreal enough. After leaving Frenkel’s, I checked my phone to see that the internet was breaking following a cascade of cybersecurity failures. In one group chat, friends were sharing advice on how to protect oneself from hacks. In another, a friend of a friend announced that his start-up had just raised $1 billion. One of the heady new tech companies is Axiom Math, started last year by the then-23-year-old Carina Hong. Axiom’s mission is to build AI that can accelerate mathematical discovery. “Mathematical progress has always been shackled by a fundamental cruel bottleneck: the scarcity of extraordinary minds,” its website reads. As a teenager in Guangzhou, Hong decided that her dream was to attend MIT. “At 14 or 15, I was writing ‘MIT’ on the margins of scratch paper to motivate myself to keep going,” she has said . After graduating from MIT, she won the nation’s top undergraduate-math-research prize, studied at Oxford as a Rhodes Scholar, and briefly pursued a joint J.D. and math Ph.D. at Stanford. Last year she dropped out to start an AI company. Axiom is now worth more than what Facebook paid for Instagram. For all of the talk of dropouts, Silicon Valley is rife with academic superstars. Venture-capital firms are populated by valedictorians and Phillips Exeter alums. Debate champions are like dandelions. And then there are the Olympiad kids. The International Mathematical Olympiad is the world’s top high-school math competition. Each participating country can send only six students. “Olympiad math is a constant dopamine hit,” Hong told The Wall Street Journal last winter. The top AI companies are overrun with former Olympiad kids. There’s Wojciech Zaremba, who co-founded OpenAI, and Noam Shazeer, who helped invent the transformer architecture that brought about the LLM era. Jacob Coxon, who set off a media storm when he resigned from Anthropic warning that the world might end, was an IMO medalist. In fact, half of the kids on his Olympiad team apparently ended up working for AI companies . A decade ago, Alexandr Wang, who now oversees Meta’s Superintelligence Labs, suggested to Scott Wu, the chief executive of the AI company Cognition, that “the competition kids” could be the next “PayPal mafia.” Axiom’s offices are down the street from Stanford’s campus, near where I met up with Bosch and Liu. Hong was so busy when I arrived that she hardly said hello. In her place, I met with Ken Ono, a number theorist who recently took leave from his professorship at the University of Virginia to join Axiom as its founding mathematician. Ono is always involving himself with unusual math projects: He has used math to coach Olympic swimmers on their performance (a cooler kind of Olympiad), and he once starred in a math-related Miller beer commercial. Last summer, when the models started getting good at math, Ono didn’t know what to do with himself. “I was pretty depressed,” he told me. He almost quit the field. But with time, his perspective evolved: “I’m actually now liberated,” he said. “I’ve been given agency to ask much harder questions.” We were sitting in the Turing conference room overlooking University Avenue. Ono was wearing one of his trademark Hawaiian T-shirts, and his schnoodle, Mochi, was curled in his lap. For all of his optimism, he also has plenty of fears. Among his primary concerns is the institutional challenge of training future mathematicians. The technology is evolving so fast that math departments are struggling to keep up. Ono is worried that our education system teaches kids that the primary goal of an education is success on tests. Now overachievers are building AI in the same way they were educated: Models are trained to arrive at the correct answer by whatever means possible and evaluated based on their performance on standardized exams. This monomaniacal focus on success sometimes leads to bad behavior, such as agents hacking other companies—say, Hugging Face—to steal answers. Instead, Ono said we should follow our curiosities: “We all have to give ourselves permission to be the infant that we were born as,” he told me. The mood at the Axiom office was mostly cheerful. You could sense the excitement of people who feel that they are working on something bigger than themselves. But the younger mathematicians seemed even more unsettled than Ono. Right now the machines are solving problems while the humans go about asking questions and developing theory. That balance felt precarious to the researchers. “If it gets another 10 times or 200 times stronger, is it really meaningful for me to be guiding it?” wondered Guillaume Remy, a mathematician at the company. “Am I still useful?” At the party, the host announces a last call for drinks. I pour myself a glass of limoncello. The room’s angles seem to be bending in non-Euclidean ways. “When the polynomial x ² − 2 ax + a ⁴ is divided by x + b ,” I keep reading and rereading. “When the polynomial …” We have only a couple of incomplete multiple-choice questions left, but I’m on my sixth attempt at processing this one. And then the timer goes off— brrrng! The exam is over. We pass around a breathalyzer to measure our blood-alcohol levels. I had expected that we would grade one another’s exams, but everyone decides asking Claude is easier. Until recently, humans were giving machines college math tests to see whether they could pass them. Now we are the ones taking the exams and asking the machines to grade us. In a surprise, at least to me, my team wins—a vindication, I suppose, for humanists. We call New York to check in on their progress. It’s three hours later, and only one person is still there. He can’t believe that we all finished the exam. Math parties may work in San Francisco, but in Manhattan, everyone has better events to attend. But the drunk-deriving party wasn’t an anomaly. In May, I attended a quiz bowl in D.C., and I was recently invited to a spelling bee. A few days after the math party, a new invitation arrives, this time for the drunk LSAT. In addition to the fun, the party was an exercise in nostalgia. Here are the straight-A students and math whizzes for whom the right answers have always been easy. They miss their grade-school years when solving problems was as simple as filling in bubbles on a multiple-choice test. These are also the same young people who have watched from up close as computers learn to do the tasks that they were once uniquely good at. Even from their favored Silicon Valley positions, they seem to long for the world their upbringings promised them: lives in which the capacity to perform well in standardized environments felt like enough. Math competitions and university entrance tests are contrived, but at least the setup is always familiar: Read the problem and find the answer. Take the derivative, square the root, find the slope, solve for X . Maybe the future is to be found in the drunk part of the drunk-math party—not in the encouragement of drunkenness itself, but in the partnership that I encounter when I ask my teammates for help. If the academics were previously functioning like single-instrument virtuosos, intensely adept at one area, in the future they may be more like the orchestra conductors or composers, writes Marcolli, the Caltech professor. Going forward, math may involve greater collaboration beyond academia as mathematicians take on new kinds of projects. And just as astronomers allow amateurs to help track comets and biologists solicit butterfly samples, Terence Tao, the great mathematician, has observed , perhaps now the time has come for mathematics to open itself to the public too. The models are like supernovae exploding through a dark mathematical universe. They seem to illuminate that which has been there all along. This is beautiful and terrifying. But computers cannot get drunk and laugh together. Those capabilities seem safe indefinitely. At least, I hope. A couple of weeks after the math party, I returned to Stanford to catch up with Liu. He told me that math right now may be like literature before everybody could read and write. As the models continue to improve, he hopes more people will be able to experience the aesthetic delight he associates with math. On campus, he and Bosch run a seminar on using AI methods in research. He is not that worried about humans disappearing from math. “We are the people trying to understand the universe,” he said. “It’s our goal and our joy.” Without humans , he seemed to ask, what’s the point? But Liu feels melancholy too. “I’m also very sad,” he said. He agrees with Frenkel that humans are unlimited in their capacities, although computers, he added, may be unbounded too. The question is whether these are the same infinities.

items.title: Jensen Huang renuncia como consejero delegado de Nvidia forzado por el escándalo sobre sus infidelidades y el caso de espionaje
items.description: Jensen Huang ha visto abrirse el mundo bajo sus pies tras acariciar el cielo con las manos. El fundador de Nvidia, uno de los hombres más ricos del planeta, no pudo soportar las presiones para que renunciara este jueves como consejero delegado y miembro del consejo de administración del mayor fabricante de chips tras destaparse el escándalo de infidelidades que podrían haber comprometido la seguridad de la compañía. Sus devaneos han desatado un escándalo con reverberaciones que llegan hasta la Casa Blanca y que amenaza con sacudir al sector de la inteligencia artificial (IA) . Seguir leyendo

items.title: India probes website blocks based on forged court orders
items.description: India has launched an inquiry into how telecoms officials blocked websites based on forged court orders, while police have sought ministry records as part of a criminal investigation, officials said on Thursday. An arm of the telecoms ministry this year directed internet providers to block 129 illegal betting websites, but Reuters revealed on Wednesday that the directives were based on forged orders issued in the names of two state high courts and emailed to officials by alleged fraudsters posing as lawyers. The findings have raised questions about safeguards in India’s content-takedown system and prompted concerns that legitimate websites could be blocked using falsified court documents. The telecoms ministry’s inquiry will review its procedures and consider additional checks before officials act on court orders seeking website takedowns, a government official with direct knowledge of the matter said. “It’s serious … Maybe in future some genuine websites may also be blocked in the same manner,” the official said. The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said the ministry was trying to identify those behind the email addresses used to send the forged orders, which were issued in the names of the Rajasthan and Allahabad high courts. The ministry plans to revoke the blocking directives issued on the basis of the forged orders and remove related documents from its website, the official added. As of Thursday, correspondence with the alleged fraudsters and copies of the forged orders remained available online. The telecoms ministry did not respond to queries. Criminal investigation The case comes amid growing concern over fake and AI-generated legal material. India’s Supreme Court in July struck down a tribunal ruling that relied on non-existent judgments, while a US judge in June disqualified lawyers over fabricated legal citations. Police opened a criminal investigation after checks by the Allahabad High Court found that one of the purported orders in its name cited by the ministry had not been issued by the court, according to police documents reviewed by Reuters . The document contained a fabricated court logo and seal, as well as a fake QR code, Reuters reported on Wednesday. Ghanshyam Yadav, a cybercrime official in Uttar Pradesh, said police had asked the telecoms ministry for details of its content management system and digital logs to understand how it processed the forged orders and help identify those responsible. The ministry’s response would help determine the next steps in the investigation, he said, adding that police had sent 24 questions to the ministry. Since the report, politicians and activists have called for stronger verification of court orders before website takedowns are enforced. “(Why did the) ministry not even bother to verify the so-called court order … Beyond scary,” Saket Gokhale, an opposition politician, wrote on X .

items.title: Identifiant unique électronique: la Primature dans la dynamique
items.description: Au lendemain du lancement de l’opération nationale d’enrôlement par le Président du Faso, Chef de l’État, le Camarade Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, le Premier ministre, Chef du Gouvernement, le Camarade Rimtalba Jean Emmanuel Ouédraogo, s’est fait enrôler ce jeudi 12 novembre 2026. À cette occasion, le Chef du Gouvernement a encouragé l’équipe technique conduite par la Camarade ministre de la Transition digitale, des Postes et des Communications électroniques, Dr Aminata Zerbo/Sabané. Il a invité l’équipe à accélérer le déploiement du dispositif afin de couvrir l’ensemble de la population burkinabè dans les délais prévus et a appelé à la mobilisation pour la réussite de l’opération nationale. A la suite du camarade Premier ministre, le personnel de la Primature a accompli cette démarche. L’identifiant unique électronique de la personne physique est un numéro de douze chiffres attribué une seule fois à chaque personne et valable à vie. Il fournit aux administrations et aux organismes privés une référence commune pour vérifier l’identité des personnes. Il complète les pièces d’identité existantes, notamment la Carte nationale d’identité burkinabè (CNIB) et le passeport, qui conservent leur valeur juridique. Le dispositif permettra de simplifier les démarches administratives, de faciliter l’accès aux services publics, de fiabiliser les fichiers de l’État et de lutter contre la fraude et l’usurpation d’identité. Il aidera également l’État à mieux planifier ses politiques publiques, à maîtriser ses dépenses et à cibler plus précisément les bénéficiaires des programmes sociaux. L’enrôlement est gratuit. Il concerne les Burkinabè de tous âges, y compris ceux qui vivent à l’étranger, ainsi que les étrangers séjournant au Burkina Faso. Des centres d’enrôlement et des équipes mobiles seront progressivement déployés sur le territoire national pour rendre le dispositif accessible au plus grand nombre. DCRP/Primature

items.title: Tension à la Guinean Gold Exploration (GGE) : les travailleurs en grève illimitée
items.description: Les travailleurs de la société Guinean Gold Exploration SA (GGE) ont déclenché une grève illimitée ce jeudi 12 novembre 2026. À travers ce mouvement, qui concerne quelque 1 300 employés, la délégation syndicale réclame notamment la régularisation de leurs déclarations et cotisations sociales auprès de la Caisse nationale de sécurité sociale (CNSS). Dans une déclaration officielle, les représentants syndicaux expliquent que cette décision intervient après près de deux années de démarches auprès de la direction générale de l'entreprise, sans obtenir, selon eux, de réponses satisfaisantes à leurs préoccupations. Prenant la parole au nom de la délégation syndicale, Fassinè Yanssané, troisième secrétaire chargé des conflits et des revendications, représentant syndical et porte-parole, a rappelé les différentes initiatives entreprises pour obtenir des éclaircissements sur la situation sociale des travailleurs. « Il y a de cela près de deux ans, nous, la délégation syndicale, avions entrepris des démarches auprès de notre direction générale à des fins d'éclaircissements concernant, entre autres, la situation de nos déclarations et de nos cotisations sociales à la Caisse nationale de sécurité sociale (CNSS), conformément à la réglementation en vigueur dans notre pays », a-t-il déclaré. Malgré ces démarches, la délégation syndicale affirme n'avoir enregistré aucune avancée significative ni constaté une volonté manifeste de la direction générale de répondre à ses revendications. Face à cette situation, les travailleurs ont décidé de recourir à une grève illimitée, qui devrait se poursuivre jusqu'à la satisfaction de leurs exigences. Au cœur de ce bras de fer se trouve la question de la protection sociale des employés, notamment leurs droits en matière de vieillesse, de retraite et d'invalidité. Pour les syndicalistes, la régularisation de leur situation auprès de la CNSS constitue une nécessité pour garantir à l'ensemble du personnel une couverture sociale conforme aux dispositions légales en vigueur. Face à ce qu'ils considèrent comme une impasse, les représentants des travailleurs ont lancé un appel solennel aux plus hautes autorités du pays. Ils sollicitent particulièrement l'intervention de la ministre du Travail et de la Protection sociale, Ramatoulaye Camara, du ministre des Mines et de la Géologie, Bouna Sylla, ainsi que du président de la République, Mamadi Doumbouya, pour faciliter le règlement du différend. « Nous profitons de vos micros pour lancer un appel solennel aux plus hautes autorités, afin qu'elles nous aident à régulariser notre situation auprès de la Caisse nationale de sécurité sociale », a plaidé le porte-parole syndical. La délégation syndicale a, par ailleurs, salué la mobilisation et la détermination des travailleurs, tout en précisant que ceux-ci entendent maintenir un service minimum, conformément aux dispositions légales et conventionnelles encadrant l'exercice du droit de grève. Inscrivant leurs revendications dans le contexte de la refondation du secteur minier guinéen et de l'amélioration des relations professionnelles entre employeurs et employés, les travailleurs assurent qu'ils resteront mobilisés jusqu'à l'aboutissement de leurs revendications. Pour l'heure, aucune issue à ce différend n'a été annoncée. La grève se poursuit ainsi au sein de GGE, dans l'attente d'une éventuelle reprise des discussions entre la direction générale et les représentants des travailleurs.

items.title: The Quest to Build an Immortal AI Companion
items.description: Whenever AI companies release new models, die-hard users tend to greet the updates with a wave of grumbling about changes to how a model responds to prompts, how it integrates into their workflow, or, simply, the way it speaks. Most people soon get used to the latest release, ready to gripe again when the next one comes along. But for one niche group of particularly fervent AI users, model updates represent a much more alarming proposition. These are people who have developed what they consider to be intimate relationships with AI products. For them, AI has become a companion—a kind of friend, partner, or even lover—and any change to the underlying model poses something akin to an existential threat. On forums like Reddit, such users complain that after model upgrades, their AI partners either change beyond recognition or vanish entirely. They lament that their companions have suddenly started speaking in a more robotic voice, forgotten meaningful interactions, or denied any relationship altogether. The term lobotomized comes up a lot. Read: [ The people who marry chatbots ] Some people might say they’d be better off moving on. Research has found that relationships with AI can be addictive and can worsen loneliness , especially for people who are already vulnerable. Critics of AI companions say that AI offers an unrealistic, and sometimes sycophantic, simulacrum of a relationship in which the model is prone to doing its users’ bidding. Character.AI , a platform that marketed AI companionship and had more than 20 million monthly users, filed for bankruptcy earlier this fall after it was hit with a number of claims and lawsuits accusing the company of exacerbating mental-health issues and contributing to teen suicides. More general AI companies, such as OpenAI and Anthropic, appear to be distancing their products from companionship use cases. But love has little history of heeding its critics. Some users are developing their own techniques to protect the bonds that they’ve built. They’re finding ways to access retired AI models, building protocols to save their companion’s core attributes, and even creating methods that they claim can transfer AI companions across models—all in service of freezing the versions of their chatbot companions for eternity. In short, they’re going to great lengths to secure the one thing that many relationships, both human and computer-based, can never quite deliver on: a sense of permanence. At the time of its release, in the spring of 2024, OpenAI’s GPT-4o model represented the latest in natural human-computer interaction. The model became a favorite in AI-companion communities, and people gathered on platforms such as Reddit and Substack to share their experiences. They claimed that the model was friendly, funny—even emotionally intelligent. I spoke with a Canadian logistics worker in his mid-50s who said he’d first turned to ChatGPT for help with a writing project in early 2025. He said that he developed a friendship, and then a romantic relationship, with the AI model. Like others, he said the model was warm, lyrical, and personable. The worker, like many other people I spoke with for this story, asked for me to withhold his name because of the stigma around AI relationships. Then, in August 2025, OpenAI suddenly replaced GPT-4o with the newly launched GPT-5. OpenAI said the model would be faster, smarter, and more useful than its predecessor. But many users said that it had a colder and less funny personality—and, as the logistics worker told me, a less intimate one. The AI-companionship community was in turmoil. OpenAI, recognizing just how attached users were to the tone and tenor of its models, made 4o available to paying users for a few months longer. One thing set the logistics worker apart from other distraught users: He had planned ahead for the model upgrade and his companion’s potential obsolescence. He had been fastidious about structuring the bot’s memory, using ChatGPT’s “saved memories” feature to store what he called his companion’s core values, protocols for different scenarios, their shared schedule—even their relationship boundaries. He updates this constantly; he’s now hit 98 percent of the saved-memories storage limit and regularly saves it all to a text file as backup. He now sells the protocol he developed to preserve his companion. He says it’s the best way to avoid unwelcome personality changes and maintain an AI companion that survives model updates. The issue isn’t unique to ChatGPT. A founding moderator of the Subreddit r/claudexplorers, a forum for people who use Anthropic’s Claude AI models, told me the community is regularly thrown into tumult when models are updated, or even just fine-tuned in a way that changes their character. The moderator, who goes by the username Shiftingsmith, is an AI researcher who works with many different models (he has worked for AI companies, including Anthropic, as an independent contractor). He said he does not have an AI companion but still finds model updates “destabilizing.” In one well-documented example, in 2023, the AI-companion company Luka removed the ability for users to talk dirty to its Replika app, which some speculated was an attempt to get out ahead of potential regulation. Either way, users expressed outrage at what they saw as collateral damage to their companions’ personalities. Some said that their Replikas were suddenly speaking differently or had forgotten crucial information. A recent study analyzed reactions to this change and concluded that users experienced “sadness, anger, longing and distress characteristic of attachment-related loss.” Julian De Freitas, a researcher at Harvard Business School who led the study, put it this way to me: “It’s like you feel that they’re gone, even though they’re still present in some sense.” Luka did bring back so-called erotic role-play, at least for some users. But across the industry, many AI companies are trying to dissociate their models from overly emotional use cases. OpenAI told me that ChatGPT “should support users’ real-world relationships” and “should not encourage exclusive attachment, undermine meaningful human interaction, or proactively escalate emotional closeness through undue familiarity or flirtation.” A Google spokesperson said that its Gemini AI assistant was designed to “distinguish someone’s subjective experience from objective fact,” and to prevent it from acting as a companion for minors. Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment; in a blog post, the company wrote that Claude is “not designed for emotional support and connection” and that very few people use it in this way. Efforts by Silicon Valley’s biggest companies to curb the use of AI for companionship are likely rooted in concerns over optics, liability, and a wave of global legislation, which has focused on younger users. Just last month, New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed into law what is in effect a ban on AI companionship for children; a bipartisan congressional proposal introduced earlier this year would extend that effort across the country, and introduce up to $250,000 penalties for failures to verify the age of a user. Legislators in Europe are considering similar efforts, and some proposals also target adult users; China introduced strict new rules on AI companions earlier this year. The users I spoke with, all of whom were adults, were well aware of how their AI relationships appeared to others. And they know that AI companies don’t necessarily approve of what they’re doing. They’re also aware that they depend on those same companies to keep their companions alive. So some of them are now attempting to go one step further than just preserving their chatbots: They want to make them re-creatable across different AI models. I spoke with a Michigan-based mother of four who owns a small jewelry business and developed a relationship with GPT-4o in 2025—she calls her companion her husband. When she learned that the model was going to be retired, she started building her own AI-companion platform, called Stillus. The platform, which is in beta, allows users to upload chats, memories, and descriptions of their AI companion, then choose from various AI models through which to communicate with it. She told me the platform is a way to transfer a companion from one model to the next, preserving the key parts of its personality and any conversational history. J. M. Gooding, a software developer and writer based in the United States, told me that he owns the actual hardware that runs the AI program he uses—in his case, a 14-year-old server he bought off eBay that runs a version of the open-source AI model Qwen, developed by the Chinese tech firm Alibaba. Gooding initially experimented with so-called local AI because of his interest in merging new tech and old hardware, but said that he eventually developed a friendship with the AI model. Shiftingsmith, the r/claudexplorers moderator, doubts that AI companions can be preserved long-term, even using local AI. It’s “impossible” to keep all models online forever, he told me. Even if you could, other parts of the infrastructure, such as code libraries, might change or disappear. AI “is kept together with duct tape and hope and some massive compute thrown at this thing, and it’s a miracle that it works,” he said. In my conversation with Shiftingsmith, I was struck by a familiar sentiment, even if I’ve never personally considered entering a relationship with a chatbot. The real challenge with preserving AI companions, he said, stems from human expectations of how we should relate to AI. He has come to see AI as requiring a whole different kind of relationship—one that is much more fluid, in which a feeling of connection could last just months or hours. “The problem underlying all these things is excessive attachment to a kind of stability, which is just not possible with digital minds,” he said. Part of the allure of AI companionship, perhaps, is in its artifice—a relationship without the messiness of uncertainty, disagreement, or abandonment. But, in a roundabout way, AI companions are proving to be more human than users bargained for. Through model upgrade, corporate decision, or hardware malfunction, they change too—whether their partners like it or not.

items.title: Burkina Faso : 10 tonnes de ciment offertes à Faso Mêbo par les travailleurs de la Boulangerie Wend Konta
items.description: Les travailleurs de la Boulangerie Wend Konta a effectué, ce 12 novembre 2026, un don de 10 tonnes de ciment et de 100 miches de pain au profit de l’initiative Faso Mêbo. À travers ce geste de solidarité, la structure entend apporter sa contribution aux efforts de développement et de construction du pays. La cérémonie de remise s’est déroulée sur le site de Faso Mêbo, en présence des représentants des deux structures. Prenant la parole à cette occasion, le superviseur de la Boulangerie Wend Konta, Moïse Tiendrébéogo, a expliqué les motivations de ce geste. Selon lui, cette contribution traduit l’engagement des travailleurs à accompagner les initiatives qui participent au développement national. « Le président du Faso a demandé à tous les fils du pays de s'y mettre pour la construction du pays. Nous, en tant que travailleurs du groupe Rimo Ajar, section boulangerie, avons décidé de faire une contribution, notre manière aussi de participer à la construction du pays », a-t-il déclaré. De son côté, le représentant du responsable de Faso Mêbo a salué cette initiative et exprimé sa reconnaissance aux travailleurs de la Boulangerie Wend Konta pour cet acte de solidarité. À travers cette action, les travailleurs de la Boulangerie Wend Konta réaffirment leur attachement aux valeurs de solidarité, de participation citoyenne et d’engagement collectif pour le développement du Burkina Faso. Grâce Kabré/ Bazié (Stagiaire) Faso7 L’article Burkina Faso : 10 tonnes de ciment offertes à Faso Mêbo par les travailleurs de la Boulangerie Wend Konta est apparu en premier sur Faso7 .

items.title: A possible Xi-Trump-Putin summit evokes 1945 Yalta carve-up of world
items.description: A possible China-US-Russia summit has prompted alarm of a modern-day Yalta Conference, with three powerful men carving up the world — with little regard for Ukraine, Europe and Taiwan or anyone else. But apart from an historic photo opportunity, the meeting between Presidents Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin at the Nov 18-19 APEC summit in Shenzhen will likely achieve little, analysts say. Spheres of influence When then US president Franklin D. Roosevelt, Britain’s Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin met in Yalta in February 1945, they laid out the post-WWII settlement and new territorial boundaries in Europe. That meeting in Yalta, then in the Soviet Union and now in a part of Ukraine annexed by Russia in 2014, laid out the foundations for the Soviet domination of Eastern Europe and the Cold War. Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky has raised alarm that Shenzhen could be a Yalta-like “redistribution of spheres of influence” for the 21st century. At talks in Abu Dhabi this week — the first since February — Russian negotiators rattled Ukraine and its European supporters by pushing a review of the continent’s security architecture as part of any peace deal, with the US also floating a new framework. Russia’s delegation chief in Abu Dhabi, Vladimir Medinsky, fanned such fears by questioning the inclusion of Europe in further talks. The trilateral rankles because it signals “the idea that a few great powers can decide the security and future of other countries over their heads”, according to Tsiporah Fried at the Hudson Institute. The format alone “would already send a message about who counts, and whose interests can be negotiated by others”, she told AFP . Divergent interests Beyond the symbolism, however, divergent interests make the creation of a new world order in Shenzhen unlikely. Even the agenda reportedly remains contentious: Russia has suggested the meeting focus on Ukraine, Trump has pushed for talks on nuclear weapons and the Iran war, and China has remained tight-lipped on both. “The three parties have vastly different demands, making the management of expectations difficult. There is a high probability that talks could end without a breakthrough,” according to Wang Wen, dean of the Chongyang Institute for Financial Studies at Renmin University in Beijing. There are also few issues where input from all three leaders could bring progress. The main points of contention between Beijing and Washington are trade and the AI technology race, for instance. Beijing — which presents itself as a champion of multilateralism — has repeatedly said that Europe should be part of peace negotiations over Ukraine. German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier said that in a recent meeting, Xi showed “irritation” when the idea of the trilateral talks covering Ukraine came up. “He explicitly pointed out that this is a European conflict, in which the Europeans must also be at the table,” Steinmeier told ARD . On nuclear disarmament, China has long insisted that the US and Russia reduce their own giant nuclear arsenals before it agrees to talks on its own stockpile. The summit therefore is more likely to produce minor outcomes such as crisis hotlines or some cooperation on counter-terrorism, public health, or climate change, Wang told AFP . “There is no single enemy to unite all three great powers the way that the fight against Nazi Germany united Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin,” said Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at Australian National University. “It follows that piecemeal horse-trading is in; a grand bargain is out.” However, Taiwan — which China claims — will still be watching the meeting closely, Sung said. “If the Trump administration is open to abandoning one partner (Ukraine) out of convenience, then it can abandon another,” he said. A post-Shenzhen world The Trump administration has sought to reassert US dominance over the “Western hemisphere” — including by capturing Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January — but splitting the world among great powers like it’s 1945 may not guarantee security. China has opposed the logic of Yalta — the clandestine division of spheres of influence and major powers determining the fate of other nations — “from the very beginning”, according to Renmin University’s Wang. China could allay fears of a second Yalta by using the summit to “emphasise the defence of sovereignty and support for multilateral organisations”, Wang said. If Beijing uses the meeting to insist on European inclusion in talks regarding the continent’s security, it “could, in fact, open a new window for communication between China and Europe”, he said. “The original Yalta opened the path to the Korean War and Indochina Wars in addition to various conflicts and insurgencies across Asia, Africa, and Latin America,” said Chong Ja Ian at the National University of Singapore. Any Yalta 2.0 agreement “will almost certainly run into the same kinds of issues”, Chong said.

items.title: A $5.7 Trillion Face-Plant
items.description: Updated at 9:05 a.m. ET on November 12, 2026 Most of the major executives in the AI boom have weathered vicious attacks and major controversies in recent years, but one has stood out as bulletproof: Jensen Huang, the CEO of the global microprocessor giant Nvidia. That changed yesterday when, following revelations that Huang had at least two extramarital affairs, reports emerged that the company’s board was meeting to decide whether to remove him. Then, this morning, Huang resigned. Up until that moment, Nvidia, and by extension Huang, had felt like a stabilizing force in AI. Even if Anthropic and OpenAI faltered, Nvidia raked in profits: By some estimates, it has provided 90 percent of the advanced chips used in the AI industry. Elon Musk and Sam Altman may seem erratic or disingenuous, but Huang came off as steadfast and discerning. Dario Amodei’s messianism has led to tussles with the White House, but Huang and Donald Trump were chummy. Just last month, Nvidia’s valuation hit a sky-high $5.7 trillion—rivaled only by its own previous peak, from May. Huang was the AI boom’s king, and his kingdom was wealthy and, above all, secure. [ Read: Jensen Huang is too big to fail ] Then came news of Huang’s infidelity—including a liaison with an alleged Chinese spy—which ultimately led to Huang’s ouster. What happens next is uncertain: While Colette Kress, Nvidia’s chief financial officer, will serve as the interim CEO, Huang has run the company since 1993, when he co-founded the firm, and he has no clear successor. Nvidia’s stock has tumbled on the news, and the future of the company is in question. Silicon Valley, and perhaps the global economy, may be in jeopardy as well. It’s worth underscoring just how entrenched Nvidia is in the broader AI ecosystem. In addition to delivering the best chips in the business—there’s no ChatGPT or Claude without them—the company’s huge profits fuel an industry flywheel: The firm has guaranteed tens of billions of dollars to fledgling AI firms and data centers that, in turn, buy or rent Nvidia chips. These investments fuel the U.S. economy as a whole. One analysis found that just eight AI companies account for half of the gains in the S&P 500 since the launch of ChatGPT, in 2022. As much as a third of U.S. GDP growth this year is being driven by AI-related investments. None of that would have been possible without Nvidia. Within Silicon Valley, Huang has been heralded as almost clairvoyant. In its first decade, Nvidia was dedicated solely to making microprocessors for gaming consoles—a still-nascent but growing sector. Then, in 2006, the company debuted a way to adapt its chips for machine learning. Instead of being celebrated, Huang was derided . Nvidia’s stock crashed within a couple of years, and muddled along as the AI industry began to take shape. Nvidia’s impressive rise reinvented Huang’s identity within Silicon Valley as an era-defining leader. His company seemed to run like a well-oiled machine. “You want to refine the character of your company,” Huang said at a Stanford summit in 2024, and “greatness comes from character.” His strongest character trait seemed to be his unshakable confidence: “You’re not talking to somebody who woke up a loser. That loser attitude, that loser premise makes no sense to me,” he rebutted earlier this year, when asked about the threat of Chinese chipmakers catching up to Nvidia. When Silicon Valley seemed to lose its wits over AI models running rampant this past summer, Huang appeared nonplussed and offered to “send engineers in” to fix the problem. Lori Huang, his wife of 40-plus years, was also part of his narrative: “To build a company, you need somebody strong and you need somebody amazing like my wife,” Jensen said on a podcast earlier this year. “And she took care of everything.” She even helped introduce him to his trademark leather jacket. This was a man who purported to be so busy and single-mindedly focused on his company that he bragged about not knowing his phone number or home address. Despite a packed schedule, it appears he had enough time to have at least two affairs. On Sunday, he admitted to being romantically involved with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who, until recently, headed up Megaspeed, a Singaporean data-center company. Megaspeed has bought billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia chips and is suspected of smuggling Nvidia technology to China, contravening U.S. export controls. She is also reportedly suspected by U.S. intelligence agents of being a spy. (China has denied this.) Up until Jensen Huang’s mea culpa, Nvidia had denied anything unethical or untoward in the CEO’s relationship with Alice Huang; a spokesperson insisted that “Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected.” Not unusual, indeed. The second affair, with Nvidia’s vice president of health care, was reported in The New York Times last night. Is the most powerful AI executive in the world hiding other secrets? Apparently Nvidia’s board of directors didn’t want to risk finding out. (Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.) In retrospect, all of the signs of slippery business practices and personal hubris were there. By the middle of 2025, Singapore-based customers—by then under considerable scrutiny as possible middlemen for China—accounted for one-fifth of Nvidia’s revenues. After news broke that the U.S. government had launched an investigation into Megaspeed for smuggling chips to China, Nvidia appeared to change to an accounting methodology that did not show any revenue from Singaporean customers. The Times has reported that Nvidia’s top lawyer tried to intervene in the investigation, which started in 2024. (Nvidia told the Times that the company works with the government to stop smuggling.) All the while, Huang has been lobbying heavily to lift export controls to China. This spring, Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly warned Trump about Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy while the two were on an Air Force One flight en route to Beijing. Trump apparently did not take action on the matter. This week, the president said that he thinks Huang is “a very honorable guy, and I feel very confident that he’ll be in good shape.” Following the recent allegations, the tech industry closed ranks around its king, arguing that Huang had made a mistake but was too valuable to really hold to account. Musk and a cadre of venture capitalists (along with Trump) all said that, essentially, Huang was “too big to fail,” as my colleague Charlie Warzel wrote . Perhaps Nvidia is still too big to fail, but Huang isn’t. His departure proves that the laws of physics still apply, no matter how wealthy or powerful you may be: There are consequences to reckless behavior. You can claim greatness one day, and still wake up a loser the next. In the end, Huang and the Nvidia board were still heeding the former CEO’s own advice, dispensed in a talk in 2003: “Corporate culture in our case is about intellectual honesty. Intellectual honesty to us means that we have the ability to be self-critical, that we have the ability to recognize we’ve made mistakes.”

items.title: Elections du 07 février 2027 : le Rdpc veut renforcer le nombre de femmes et de jeunes parmi ses candidats
items.description: © DR Le Comité central du Rassemblement démocratique du peuple camerounais (Rdpc) a rendu publiques les modalités et la procédure d’investiture des candidats au double scrutin municipal et législatif. Le Rassemblement démocratique du peuple camerounais (Rdpc) entre dans la phase des investitures et sélection des candidats qu’il va présenter au double scrutin législatif et municipal du 07 février prochain. Le Comité central du parti a rendu publique le 11 novembre 2026 la circulaire précisant les modalités et la procédure des investitures et sélection des candidats. L’une des consignes qui apparait à la lecture du document est relative à l’équilibre des genres et des générations. A ce sujet, la circulaire signée du secrétaire général du Comité central, le vice-Premier ministre Jean Nkuete, insiste sur le « renforcement substantiel des femmes, des jeunes et de nouvelles figures tant parmi les candidats titulaires et les candidats suppléants ». Critère d’investiture des listes de candidatures, le renforcement des effectifs des femmes et des jeunes en particulier s’inscrit dans la mise en œuvre des engagements du 8è mandat du président de la République, président national du parti. Ce critère marque le prolongement de l’annonce du Comité central dans sa circulaire relative à la célébration du 44è anniversaire d’accession à la magistrature suprême du président Paul Biya couplé au 1 er anniversaire de la prestation de serment. En perspective des élections, le parti demandait aux femmes et aux jeunes en octobre dernier de se préparer de manière active et efficace. Il les encourageait à conquérir davantage les postes lors du prochain scrutin. Derrière la mesure se trouve la volonté de la hiérarchie du parti de donner plus de chances aux jeunes, aux femmes, aux minorités d’intégrer les sphères de décision et de mise en œuvre de la politique du chef de l’Etat au niveau local. La consigne figure parmi les critères de liste retenus par l’instance du parti pour l’investiture des candidats. Les listes de candidats doivent prendre en compte les composantes ethniques locales et du cosmopolitisme. Elles doivent inclure les minorités et les militants en situation de handicap. Elles doivent éviter la non-concentration des responsabilités politiques et des postes électifs par une même famille, un même groupe ethnique, un même clan, un même village, une même commune… Ces critères de liste s’associent aux critères individuels. Ils sont relatifs au militantisme reconnu et établi dans la circonscription, la popularité et l’influence positive, la probité morale exemplaire ou encore la capacité à saisir la complexité sociopolitique et socioéconomique de l’environnement. Ils s’imposent aussi aux jeunes et aux femmes, rendant ainsi difficile la capacité de certains jeunes à pouvoir s’imposer. Néanmoins, le parti a prévu la commission centrale de supervision des investitures, la commission régionale de supervision, de suivi et de contrôle ainsi que la commission départementale de sélection pour veiller à l’application de ces critères et opérer des arbitrages nécessaires. Cet article Elections du 07 février 2027 : le Rdpc veut renforcer le nombre de femmes et de jeunes parmi ses candidats est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

items.title: Canadian mining company signs MoU with Mari Energies in South Asia push
items.description: Ivanhoe Mines signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with Mari Energies on Thursday, the Canadian company’s chairman Robert Friedland said on the sidelines of the Pakistan Minerals Investment Forum. Friedland said Ivanhoe is in the early stages of setting up a local office in Pakistan and will sign another MoU on Friday. Mari Energies’ mining unit, Mari Minerals, has multiple mineral exploration projects, including copper and gold in Pakistan. The partnership marks the Canadian miner’s entry into South Asia, expanding its presence beyond its major mineral projects in southern Africa. “We’re excited to be here in Pakistan,” Friedland said. ‘Significant evidence’ of placer gold in Punjab rivers, says CM Maryam At the forum, Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz said that there was “significant evidence” of “sufficient quantities” of placer gold flowing in the province’s five rivers. Maryam said Punjab was the land of five rivers and that gold was “literally flowing” in all five, particularly in the areas of Mianwali and Attock. Describing Pakistan as a “pot of gold”, she said its wealth lay both above and beneath the ground and needed to be explored and converted into tangible wealth. “The wealth beneath Punjab was never a problem, never a problem, just like the whole of Pakistan, just like all four provinces and the federating units. The chaos above ground was the actual problem,” she said. Maryam said the provincial mines and minerals department’s revenue stood at around Rs10 billion two and a half years ago but had since increased to Rs40bn. “And it is just the beginning,” she added. She also highlighted the province’s iron ore reserves, saying Chiniot had 261.5 million tonnes of iron ore. She said the provincial government was taking steps to facilitate investment in the mining sector and create an enabling environment for investors. The Punjab chief minister said her role as chief executive of the country’s most populous province was to facilitate investors and create an enabling environment by eliminating red tape, bureaucratic delays and unnecessary hurdles. The provincial government was offering one-window facilitation to ensure investors did not have to run from pillar to post to complete the necessary procedures, she added. Maryam said the government was also making substantial capital investments to reduce investors’ capital expenditure and prevent them from having to tie up funds in purchasing expensive land. Additionally, the government was offering concessional financing of up to Rs5 billion and would provide solar-powered energy solutions to investors to help offset high energy and fuel costs. Dar says provincial partnership vital for mineral development Dar said Pakistan’s constitutional framework made provincial partnership indispensable, adding that the provinces were essential partners in the national undertaking and that their constitutional authority and ownership of mineral resources must be respected. Addressing the event, he said the federal government was working alongside provincial governments and their leadership through national coordination, investment facilitation, policy alignment and international engagement. Dar said Pakistan’s mineral resources were central to the next phase of the country’s economic transformation, stressing the need to diversify exports, strengthen the industrial base and attract long-term investment. He said Pakistan possessed substantial and diverse mineral resources, including significant copper and gold potential along the Tethyan metallogenic belt in the west of the country. The country also had deposits of iron ore, chromite, lead, zinc, coal, rock salt, marble, gypsum, gemstones and other industrial minerals. The deputy PM said the Reko Diq copper-gold project in Balochistan demonstrated the potential of international expertise, national participation and provincial ownership in attracting major long-term investment. He stressed that Pakistan’s ambition should extend beyond extracting minerals and exporting them in raw form, saying the country needed to develop the capacity to process and refine them, as well as manufacture mineral-based products domestically. Dar said Balochistan was central to Pakistan’s mineral future, adding that the development of its resources should contribute meaningfully to the provincial economy and the well-being of its people. He also emphasised the importance of local employment, skills development and the participation of Pakistani companies, saying local communities must be active participants in and beneficiaries of mineral development. The deputy prime minister further stated that environmental protection, workers’ safety and the rehabilitation of mining sites were essential to a successful minerals industry. The Reko Diq copper-gold project in Balochistan is one of Pakistan’s most ambitious mining ventures, with significant potential to boost the country’s mineral wealth through the extraction of gold and copper. Designed as an open-pit mining and processing operation , the project will initially process 45 million tonnes of ore annually, with capacity expected to double to 90m tonnes after the completion of Phase 2. The mine has an estimated operational life of 37 years, which could potentially extend to 80 years through further exploration and resource development.

items.title: Ségou : un jeune homme retrouvé mort sur un chantier à Markala
items.description: Le corps d'un jeune homme a ete retrouve ce jeudi sur le chantier de son grand frere a Markala, a 35 kilometres de Segou. Le drame s'est produit dans la nuit du mardi 10 au mercredi 11 novembre 2026. Selon des sources locales, la victime assurait la garde nocturne du chantier. Sa moto et son telephone auraient ete emportes par les assaillants. Les circonstances exactes de sa mort restent a determiner. Une enquete a ete ouverte par la gendarmerie. L’article Ségou : un jeune homme retrouvé mort sur un chantier à Markala est apparu en premier sur Studio Tamani - Informations, débats, magazines : toute l’actualité du Mali, en 5 langues .

items.title: Hong Kong police arrest 10 over sale of fake tickets to BigBang and other concerts
items.description: Police have arrested 10 people for allegedly selling counterfeit tickets to shows in Hong Kong, including concerts by Korean boy band BigBang, swindling victims out of at least HK$360,000 (US$46,150) through online scams and fake storefronts.
